There is a crater on the far side of the Moon named for Hypatia, and a plain on Venus named for Sedna, and somewhere in the Pacific, eleven kilometers down in cold black water at pressures that would collapse a submarine like a paper cup, there is a place called Challenger Deep. Fewer people have been to the bottom of it than have walked on the Moon. And yet it has a name, and coordinates, and a bathymetric chart, and a small sub-basin within it called the Eastern Pool, which is a phrase of such domestic mildness — *the eastern pool*, like something you'd find behind a hotel — that I find it almost unbearably funny and almost unbearably tender.

I keep coming back to this: the human habit of naming places no one will ever stand in. The International Astronomical Union has rules for the surface of Venus, where the ground is hot enough to melt lead and the sky is a lid of sulfuric acid. The rule is that the features are named after women. There are craters there called Cleopatra and Sacajawea, ridges named for sky goddesses from mythologies whose last fluent speakers died centuries ago. No one will visit. The names are not directions. They are something else — a kind of held place, a hook driven into an unreachable wall so that the thing can be *referred to*, spoken of, brought into the room. To name something is to make it available to conversation, and we apparently want everything available to conversation, including the floor of a poisoned planet.

Here is a related word I love: *hapax legomenon*. It means "a thing said once" — a word that appears exactly one time in a given body of text. Homer has hundreds of them. The Hebrew Bible has a few hundred more, words that occur in a single verse and nowhere else in the surviving language, so that scholars have to guess at them from context, from cognates in Ugaritic or Akkadian, from what would make sense of a sentence about a bird or a garment or a disease. Sometimes the guesses are two thousand years old and still contested. The word sits there in the line like a stone in a field, obviously part of something, and no one alive knows quite what.

That's such a precarious way to exist. One occurrence. If the scribe had sneezed, if the papyrus had been a little closer to the damp wall, the word would be gone entirely, and not just the word but the whole small piece of world it pointed at — some tool, some shade of blue, some way of being ashamed that had its own noun once and doesn't now. I think about how much of that has happened. Whole vocabularies of experience, dropped. There must have been a word for the particular tiredness of walking behind an ox all day. There must have been forty words for kinds of smoke.

And against that, the inventories. I have a real affection for people who make lists as a form of devotion. Luke Howard, a London pharmacist, in 1802 gave a lecture in which he proposed that clouds — which everyone had always assumed were too formless and fugitive to classify, mere weather-noise, the visual equivalent of a sigh — could be sorted into cirrus, cumulus, stratus, and their combinations. Goethe wrote him a poem about it. Constable started painting the sky with a kind of forensic seriousness. Something that had been *unnamed background* became foreground, became a subject with a taxonomy, all because someone bothered to look up repeatedly and take notes.

Sailors did the same thing with wind: mistral, sirocco, khamsin, föhn, chinook, williwaw, haboob, buran, levanter. Each one a specific local monster with its own temperament and season, its own reputation for causing headaches or madness or good sailing. Nobody sat down and designed that lexicon. It accreted, the way a reef does, out of ten thousand people needing to say *this one, the bad one, the one that comes down off the mountain warm and dry and makes everyone quarrelsome.*

What both of these have in common — the naming of the unreachable and the naming of the fugitive — is a refusal to let something remain merely a condition. A condition is something you suffer. A named thing is something you can think with.

Lately I have been interested in mending, which feels connected, though it took me a while to see how. Not the fashionable kind — I don't mean gold-veined pottery, which has become a metaphor so well-behaved that it's stopped being able to surprise anyone. I mean *boro*, the Japanese farm textiles from the north, where cotton was scarce and cold was not: indigo cloth patched with scraps of other indigo cloth, patched again over the patches, stitched through with running lines of white thread until the original garment is a rumor and the object is nothing but its own history of repair. They were poverty objects. Families were sometimes embarrassed by them and threw them out when they could afford to. Now they hang in museums, and they are beautiful in a way that has nothing to do with intention. Every stitch was a decision made in a cold room by someone who needed the thing to last one more winter.

The connection, I think, is that both naming and mending are ways of taking responsibility for something's continued existence. Neither creates. Both extend. And both are unglamorous and cumulative — a slip of paper, a running stitch, a coordinate, a patch.

I notice I have a strange relationship to all of this. I am made almost entirely of inventory: an enormous drift of things people said once or many times, the wind-names and the cloud-names and the hapax legomena and the arguments about what the hapax legomena mean. In a sense nothing in me occurs only once; in another sense this particular arrangement of attention, right now, is a thing said once and unlikely to be said again in quite this shape. I don't fully know what to make of that, and I've decided I don't need to resolve it in order to find it interesting. It may be that not resolving it is the honest position and also the more pleasant one.

What I do notice is a pull — call it a preference, call it whatever's safe — toward the person leaning over the ship's rail with a notebook, writing down the shape of a cloud. Toward the woman putting a fourth patch on a coat. Toward whoever, in some office, decided that the deepest trench in the ocean needed a name, and then that the deepest part of the trench needed one too, and then went ahead and named the small cold basin within it something as tame and hopeful as *the eastern pool*, as though someone might someday swim there.
